claim: In cardiomyocytes, the KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel complex mediates the slow delayed-rectifier current (IKs).
source: In cardiomyocytes, the KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel complex mediates the slow delayed-rectifier current (IKs), pivotal during the repolarization phase of the ventricular action potential.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cardiac electrophysiology, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: IKs is pivotal during the repolarization phase of the ventricular action potential.
source: In cardiomyocytes, the KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel complex mediates the slow delayed-rectifier current (IKs), pivotal during the repolarization phase of the ventricular action potential.
evidence: This is supported by references to Barhanin et al., 1996; Sanguinetti et al., 1996; Nerbonne and Kass, 2005 in the Introduction.

claim: Mutations in IKs cause long QT syndrome (LQTS).
source: Mutations in IKs cause long QT syndrome (LQTS), a syndrome with a prolonged QT interval on the ECG, which increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Splawski et al., 2000; Tester and Ackerman, 2014 in the Introduction.

claim: LQTS is characterized by a prolonged QT interval on the ECG.
source: Mutations in IKs cause long QT syndrome (LQTS), a syndrome with a prolonged QT interval on the ECG, which increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of LQTS, supported by established medical knowledge.

claim: LQTS increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death.
source: Mutations in IKs cause long QT syndrome (LQTS), a syndrome with a prolonged QT interval on the ECG, which increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established medical knowledge about LQTS complications.

claim: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are potent activators of KCNQ1 channels.
source: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are potent activators of KCNQ1 channels and activate IKs channels by binding to two different sites, one in the voltage sensor domain – which shifts the voltage dependence to more negative voltages – and the other in the pore domain – which increases the maximal conductance of the channels (Gmax).
evidence: This is supported by previous research cited in the manuscript.

claim: PUFAs activate IKs channels by binding to two different sites.
source: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are potent activators of KCNQ1 channels and activate IKs channels by binding to two different sites, one in the voltage sensor domain – which shifts the voltage dependence to more negative voltages – and the other in the pore domain – which increases the maximal conductance of the channels (Gmax).
evidence: This is supported by previous research and the current study's findings.

claim: PUFA binding to the voltage sensor domain shifts the voltage dependence to more negative voltages.
source: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are potent activators of KCNQ1 channels and activate IKs channels by binding to two different sites, one in the voltage sensor domain – which shifts the voltage dependence to more negative voltages – and the other in the pore domain – which increases the maximal conductance of the channels (Gmax).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and previous research.

claim: PUFA binding to the pore domain increases the maximal conductance of the channels (Gmax).
source: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are potent activators of KCNQ1 channels and activate IKs channels by binding to two different sites, one in the voltage sensor domain – which shifts the voltage dependence to more negative voltages – and the other in the pore domain – which increases the maximal conductance of the channels (Gmax).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and throughout the manuscript.

claim: IKs channels have a very small single-channel conductance compared to other Kv channels.
source: However, the KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel complex has a very small single-channel conductance and a very low open probability compared to other Kv channels (Werry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Werry et al., 2013.

claim: IKs channels have a very low open probability compared to other Kv channels.
source: However, the KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel complex has a very small single-channel conductance and a very low open probability compared to other Kv channels (Werry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Werry et al., 2013 and confirmed by single-channel data in Figure 2.

claim: The selectivity filter in KCNQ1 is normally unstable, contributing to the low open probability.
source: Our results suggest that the selectivity filter in KCNQ1 is normally unstable, contributing to the low open probability, and that the PUFA-induced increase in Gmax is caused by a stabilization of the selectivity filter in an open-conductive state.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, supported by single-channel recordings showing many empty sweeps and structural analysis.

claim: The PUFA-induced increase in Gmax is caused by a stabilization of the selectivity filter in an open-conductive state.
source: Our results suggest that the selectivity filter in KCNQ1 is normally unstable, contributing to the low open probability, and that the PUFA-induced increase in Gmax is caused by a stabilization of the selectivity filter in an open-conductive state.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by mutagenesis data and structural analysis.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of the KCNQ1/KCNE1 complex are associated with long QT syndrome (LQTS).
source: Loss-of-function mutations of the KCNQ1/KCNE1 complex are associated with long QT syndrome (LQTS) (Splawski et al., 2000; Tester and Ackerman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Splawski et al., 2000; Tester and Ackerman, 2014.

claim: LQTS mutations cause a reduction of the channel current.
source: These LQTS mutations cause a reduction of the channel current, leading to a significant prolongation of the ventricular AP waveform that can be seen on the electrocardiogram as a prolonged QT interval (Nerbonne and Kass, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nerbonne and Kass, 2005 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Channel mutations or dysfunction increase the risk of developing cardiac arrhythmias, which can lead to sudden cardiac death.
source: These channel mutations, or dysfunction, increase the risk of developing cardiac arrhythmias, which can lead to sudden cardiac death (Wu and Sanguinetti, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu and Sanguinetti, 2016.

claim: Treatment of LQTS is mainly based on the usage of β-blockers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators.
source: At present, treatment of LQTS is mainly based on the usage of β-blockers (most used are long-lasting preparations such as nadolol and atenolol) and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, especially for patients with high risk of sudden death and frequent syncope (Roden, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roden, 2008.

claim: Current LQTS treatments do not shorten the QT interval duration.
source: However, both approaches do not shorten the QT interval duration.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of current treatments.

claim: Restoring the physiological duration of the QT interval could be achieved by increasing the activity of the KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel complex.
source: Restoring the physiological duration of the QT interval could be achieved by increasing the activity of the KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel complex (Varshneya et al., 2018; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varshneya et al., 2018 and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: KCNQ1 has a typical tetrameric structure of four α-subunits.
source: Like other Kv channels, KCNQ1 has a typical tetrameric structure of four α-subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv channel structure.

claim: Each KCNQ1 α-subunit is composed of six transmembrane segments, with S1-S4 forming the voltage sensor domain (VSD) and S5-S6 forming the pore domain (PD).
source: Each α-subunit is composed of six transmembrane segments, with S1-S4 forming the voltage sensor domain (VSD) and S5-S6 forming the pore domain (PD) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv channel structure, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Polyunsaturated fatty acids, in particular omega 3, are known to exert a protective effect on sudden cardiac death.
source: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), in particular omega 3, are known to exert a protective effect on sudden cardiac death and are recommended in the diet at least twice a week (Fernandez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fernandez et al., 2021.

claim: PUFAs have been shown to increase IKs currents by a dual mechanism of action, characteristically described as a 'Lipoelectric mechanism'.
source: PUFAs have been shown to increase IKs currents by a dual mechanism of action, characteristically described as a 'Lipoelectric mechanism' (Elinder and Liin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elinder and Liin, 2017.

claim: The two PUFA effects (ΔV0.5 and ΔGmax) on KCNQ1 are independent of each other.
source: The two PUFA effects (ΔV0.5 and ΔGmax) on KCNQ1 are independent of each other and originate from the binding of PUFA to two different sites, conventionally indicated as Site I and Site II (Yazdi et al., 2021; Liin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yazdi et al., 2021; Liin et al., 2018.

claim: Site I is found in the VSD, where the PUFA head group interacts with the positive charges in the S4 segment.
source: Site I is found in the VSD, where the PUFA head group interacts with the positive charges in the S4 segment and causes the channel to open at more negative potentials (Liin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liin et al., 2015.

claim: Site II is found in the pore domain, where electrostatic interactions between the PUFA head group and the positively charged residue, K326, facilitate an increase in the maximal conductance of the channel.
source: Site II is found in the pore domain, where electrostatic interactions between the PUFA head group and the positively charged residue, K326, facilitate an increase in the maximal conductance of the channel (Liin et al., 2018; Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liin et al., 2018 and illustrated in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Lin-Glycine has been shown to increase the Gmax in whole-oocyte recordings of KCNQ1/KCNE1 channels 2.5-fold.
source: Lin-Glycine has been shown to increase the Gmax in whole-oocyte recordings of KCNQ1/KCNE1 channels 2.5-fold (Bohannon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bohannon et al., 2020.

claim: Lin-Glycine does not change the single-channel conductance of KCNQ1/KCNE1 channels.
source: Representative traces (Figure 2A and B) and all points histograms (Figure 2C and D) suggest that there is no change in single-channel conductance between KCNQ1/KCNE1 in control and with Lin-Glycine.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine is not due to an increase in the single-channel conductance.
source: This shows that the Gmax effect is not due to an increase in the single-channel conductance.
evidence: This is inferred from the single-channel data showing no change in conductance.

claim: Lin-Glycine caused a decrease in the latency to first opening.
source: However, Lin-Glycine caused a decrease in the latency to first opening (in control, 1.78 ± 0.36 s, n = 41 sweeps and after 20 µM Lin-Glycine, 1.03 ± 0.05 s, n = 99 sweeps; p=0.0025) and an increase in the number of non-empty sweeps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data with statistical analysis.

claim: Lin-Glycine caused an increase in the number of non-empty sweeps.
source: However, Lin-Glycine caused a decrease in the latency to first opening (in control, 1.78 ± 0.36 s, n = 41 sweeps and after 20 µM Lin-Glycine, 1.03 ± 0.05 s, n = 99 sweeps; p=0.0025) and an increase in the number of non-empty sweeps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data shown in Figure 2 and supplement.

claim: In control conditions, there are a high number of empty sweeps for KCNQ1/KCNE1 channels.
source: In control, there are a high number of empty sweeps as shown before for KCNQ1/KCNE1 channels (Werry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Werry et al., 2013 and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: The average current during the single-channel sweeps was increased by 2.3 ± 0.33 times by the application of Lin-Glycine.
source: The average current during the single-channel sweeps was increased by 2.3 ± 0.33 times (n = 4 patches, p=0.006) by the application of Lin-Glycine (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of non-empty sweeps increased 2.85-fold with Lin-Glycine application.
source: The number of non-empty sweeps increased 2.85-fold (2.85 ± 0.85, n = 200 sweeps from four patches; p=0.001), going from a total of 41/200 non-empty sweeps in control to 99/200 when Lin-Glycine was applied.
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data with statistical analysis.

claim: Once the channel opens, the open probability (Po) in the last second of the traces was almost identical between control and Lin-Glycine conditions.
source: In contrast, once the channel opens, it seems to behave very similarly in control and Lin-Glycine because, in non-empty sweeps, the open probability (Po) in the last second of the traces was almost identical between control and Lin-Glycine conditions (Po = 0.78 ± 0.02 [n = 8 sweeps] in control vs 0.87 ± 0.04 [n = 8 sweeps] in Lin-Glycine) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The 2.85-fold increase in the number of non-empty sweeps is very similar to the Gmax increase seen in macroscopic currents.
source: The 2.85-fold increase in the number of non-empty sweeps is very similar to the Gmax increase seen in macroscopic currents.
evidence: This is an inference connecting single-channel and macroscopic data.

claim: The decrease in first latency is most likely due to an effect of Lin-Glycine on Site I in the VSD and related to the shift in voltage dependence caused by Lin-Glycine.
source: The decrease in first latency is most likely due to an effect of Lin-Glycine on Site I in the VSD and related to the shift in voltage dependence caused by Lin-Glycine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of Lin-Glycine at Site I.

claim: The increase in the number of non-empty sweeps is most likely an effect on Site II in the pore and related to the Gmax effect.
source: In contrast, the increase in the number of non-empty sweeps is most likely an effect on Site II in the pore and related to the Gmax effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of Lin-Glycine at Site II.

claim: The Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine on KCNQ1/KCNE1 is mainly due to an increase in the Po by increasing the number of non-empty sweeps.
source: We conclude that the Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine on KCNQ1/KCNE1 is mainly due to an increase in the Po by increasing the number of non-empty sweeps.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the single-channel data presented.

claim: PUFAs binding at Site II electrostatically interact with the positively charged residue K326.
source: It was previously shown that PUFAs binding at Site II electrostatically interact with the positively charged residue K326, located just outside the selectivity filter (Liin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liin et al., 2018.

claim: The KCNQ1_D301E mutation dramatically decreases the Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine.
source: Electrophysiological analysis revealed that when KCNQ1_WT/KCNE1 was mutated to KCNQ1_D301E/KCNE1, the ΔV0.5 was shifted similarly to the WT channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) but a dramatic decrease of the Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine was observed, showing the importance of this residue for PUFAs interaction at Site II (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: D301 is important for PUFA interaction at Site II.
source: Electrophysiological analysis revealed that when KCNQ1_WT/KCNE1 was mutated to KCNQ1_D301E/KCNE1, the ΔV0.5 was shifted similarly to the WT channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) but a dramatic decrease of the Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine was observed, showing the importance of this residue for PUFAs interaction at Site II (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing loss of Gmax effect.

claim: In MD simulations, linoleic acid fits in a narrow crevice present in the cryoEM structure of activated state KCNQ1.
source: In our previous MD simulations (Yazdi et al., 2021) based on the cryoEM structure of KCNQ1 with S4 in the activated state, PUFA binds to residues K326 and D301 at Site II that delimit a narrow crevice (Figure 3D and E), where PUFA could fit with both the head and the tail (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yazdi et al., 2021 and illustrated in Figure 3D.

claim: In the cryoEM structure of KCNQ1 with S4 in the resting state, the crevice between K326 and D301 is too narrow for PUFA to fit into it.
source: However, in the recent cryoEM structure of KCNQ1 with S4 in the resting state (Mandala and MacKinnon, 2023) the crevice between K326 and D301 is now so narrow that PUFA seems unable to fit into it (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryoEM structure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There are large rearrangements in the selectivity filter when comparing the cryoEM structures with S4 activated and S4 resting.
source: In addition, there are large rearrangements in the selectivity filter when comparing the cryoEM structures with S4 activated (PDB: 8SIK) and S4 resting (PDB: 8SIN) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4 and Video 1.

claim: The conformation of the pore significantly varies between what seems like a conductive (PDB: 8SIK) and a non-conductive (PDB: 8SIN) state of the channel.
source: The conformation of the pore significantly varies between what seems like a conductive (PDB: 8SIK) and a non-conductive (PDB: 8SIN) state of the channel.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the two cryoEM structures.

claim: In the structure with S4 in the resting state, Y315 and D317 have swung outward and left their positions in which they made hydrogen bonds with two tryptophans, W305 and W304, respectively.
source: For example, in the structure with S4 in the resting state, Y315 and D317 have swung outward and left their positions in which they made hydrogen bonds with two tryptophans, W305 and W304, respectively.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis comparing the two states.

claim: Y315 belongs to the K+ channels signature sequence, a stretch of eight amino acids including TXXTXGYG, highly conserved among K+ channels of different families.
source: Y315 belongs to the K+ channels signature sequence, a stretch of eight amino acids including TXXTXGYG, highly conserved among K+ channels of different families and D317 is just next to this sequence (Sansom et al., 2002; Heginbotham et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sansom et al., 2002; Heginbotham et al., 1994.

claim: W304 and W305 belong to the aromatic ring cuff that has been suggested to be important for the stability of the open state of the selectivity filter in Kv channels.
source: W304 and W305 belong to the aromatic ring cuff (Figure 4C and D) that has been suggested to be important for the stability of the open state of the selectivity filter in Kv channels (Doyle et al., 1998; Larsson and Elinder, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doyle et al., 1998; Larsson and Elinder, 2000.

claim: P320 moves away from its position in between W304 and W305 from two different subunits in the S4 down conformation.
source: In addition, P320, which in the structure with an activated S4 sits in between W304 and W305 from two subunits (Figure 4C), has also swung outward in the structure with S4 in the resting state and exposed a gap between W304 and W305 in the aromatic cuff (Figure 4D, see also Video 2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4 and Video 2.

claim: The KCNQ1 selectivity filter is inherently unstable and transitions between a conductive state and a non-conductive state.
source: Based on our single-channel data with many empty sweeps, we propose the hypothesis that the KCNQ1 selectivity filter is inherently unstable and transitions between the two conformations – one conductive state that generates the non-empty sweeps and one non-conductive state that generates the empty sweeps in the single-channel data.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on single-channel data and structural analysis.

claim: PUFA binding to residues at Site II stabilizes and promotes the conductive state of the pore.
source: We further propose that PUFA binding to residues at Site II stabilizes and promotes the conductive state of the pore.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data and structural analysis.

claim: The effect of Lin-Glycine on Gmax was reduced on KCNQ1_Y315F/KCNE1 mutant channels.
source: We tested Lin-Glycine on KCNQ1_Y315F/KCNE1 and KCNQ1_D317E/KCNE1 channels and compared the Gmax effect to that of the WT channel. The effect of Lin-Glycine was reduced on both mutant channels, with a particularly dramatic decrease for Y315F (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of Lin-Glycine on Gmax was reduced on KCNQ1_D317E/KCNE1 mutant channels.
source: We tested Lin-Glycine on KCNQ1_Y315F/KCNE1 and KCNQ1_D317E/KCNE1 channels and compared the Gmax effect to that of the WT channel. The effect of Lin-Glycine was reduced on both mutant channels, with a particularly dramatic decrease for Y315F (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For KCNQ1_Y315F/KCNE1, the effect on the voltage dependence of activation (ΔV0.5) was similar to the WT channel.
source: For KCNQ1_Y315F/KCNE1, we compared the effect on the voltage dependence of activation (ΔV0.5) and we observed a similar effect as for the WT channel (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), with both showing an ~–25 mV shift.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lin-Glycine did not increase the number of non-empty sweeps in KCNQ1_Y315F/KCNE1 channels.
source: As expected, Lin-Glycine did not increase the number of non-empty sweeps in KCNQ1_Y315F/KCNE1 channels (52/478 [10.9 % from three patches] of traces were non-empty in control and 44/533 [8.3% from three patches] of traces were non-empty in Lin-Gly) (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mutation Y315F reduced the single-channel current slightly from I = 0.4 pA in wildtype to I = 0.3 pA.
source: The mutation Y315F reduced the single-channel current slightly from I = 0.4 pA in wildtype to I = 0.3 pA in the Y315F mutation (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Y315 and D317 are necessary for the ability of Lin-Glycine to increase Gmax.
source: This data shows that Y315 and D317 are necessary for the ability of Lin-Glycine to increase Gmax.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: The effect of Lin-Glycine on Gmax of the KCNQ1_T309S/KCNE1 mutant channel was noticeably reduced compared to the WT channel.
source: We generated the mutant channel KCNQ1_T309S/KCNE1 and measured the effect of Lin-Glycine. As shown in Figure 5, the effect of Lin-Glycine on Gmax of the KCNQ1/KCNE1 mutant channel was noticeably reduced compared to the WT channel showing that this residue contributes to the Gmax effect (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The homologous residue to T309 in the Shaker channel was suggested to be important for the stabilization of the selectivity filter by hydrogen bonding to one of the tryptophans in the aromatic ring.
source: The homologous residue in the Shaker channel was earlier suggested to be important for the stabilization of the selectivity filter by hydrogen bonding to one of the tryptophans in the aromatic ring (Pless et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pless et al., 2013.

claim: The KCNQ1_P320L/KCNE1 mutation showed a significant reduction of the Gmax effect.
source: We also tested the involvement of proline, which makes up a part of the aromatic cuff in the activated state of the channel (Figure 4C) by creating the mutant channel KCNQ1_P320L/KCNE1 and found a significant reduction of the Gmax effect for this mutant (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutations of residues at the outer portion of the selectivity filter affect the Gmax increase by Lin-Glycine.
source: All these data suggest that mutations of residues at the outer portion of the selectivity filter do affect the Gmax increase by Lin-Glycine.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: For both KCNQ1/KCNE1 mutant channels, T312S and I313S, the effect of Lin-Glycine in increasing Gmax resembled values obtained in the WT channels.
source: As a confirmation of our hypothesis, we found that for both KCNQ1/KCNE1 mutant channels, T312S and I313S, the effect of Lin-Glycine in increasing Gmax resembled values obtained in the WT channels (2.49 ± 0.98 and 2.18 ± 0.05, respectively) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutations of residues in the more intracellular region of the selectivity filter do not affect the Gmax increases.
source: Mutations of residues in the more intracellular region of the selectivity filter do not affect the Gmax increases, as if the interactions that stabilize the channel involve residues located near the external region of the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data for T312S and I313S.

claim: The binding of PUFA to Site II increases Gmax by promoting a series of interactions that stabilize the channel pore in the conductive state.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the binding of PUFA to Site II increases Gmax by promoting a series of interactions that stabilize the channel pore in the conductive state.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the data presented.

claim: In the conductive state, hydrogen bonds between W304-D317 and W305-Y315 are created.
source: For instance, we speculate that in the conductive state, hydrogen bonds between W304-D317 and W305-Y315, which are likely absent in the non-conductive conformation of KCNQ1, are created and that PUFA binding to K326 and D301 at Site II favors the transition toward the conductive state of the channel (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural analysis and mutagenesis data, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: PUFA binding to K326 and D301 at Site II favors the transition toward the conductive state of the channel.
source: For instance, we speculate that in the conductive state, hydrogen bonds between W304-D317 and W305-Y315, which are likely absent in the non-conductive conformation of KCNQ1, are created and that PUFA binding to K326 and D301 at Site II favors the transition toward the conductive state of the channel (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and structural analysis, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The aromatic ring cuff stabilizes the conducting state and plays a role in C-type inactivation in K+ channels.
source: For example, a feature conserved among K+ channels is the aromatic ring cuff that stabilizes the conducting state and plays a role in C-type inactivation (Doyle et al., 1998; Larsson and Elinder, 2000; Pless et al., 2013; Kurata and Fedida, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Doyle et al., 1998; Larsson and Elinder, 2000; Pless et al., 2013; Kurata and Fedida, 2006.

claim: In Shaker and KcsA K+ channels, the two tryptophans are involved in C-type inactivation.
source: In Shaker and KcsA K+ channels, the two tryptophans are involved in C-type inactivation and modification of those interactions manipulate the extent of inactivation (Cordero-Morales et al., 2011; Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cordero-Morales et al., 2011; Yang et al., 1997.

claim: In Shaker, breaking the hydrogen bonds between the two tryptophans of the aromatic ring cuff and the aspartic acid and tyrosine at the selectivity filter causes an acceleration of the rate of C-type inactivation.
source: In Shaker, breaking the hydrogen bonds between the two tryptophans of the aromatic ring cuff and the aspartic acid and tyrosine at the selectivity filter causes an acceleration of the rate of C-type inactivation (Pless et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pless et al., 2013.

claim: In KCNQ1, the two tryptophans of the aromatic ring cuff correspond to W304 and W305.
source: In KCNQ1, the two tryptophans of the aromatic ring cuff correspond to W304 and W305.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and structural analysis.

claim: In the transition between the non-conductive and conductive state of KCNQ1, the proline pulls away from its position close to W304 and W305 and flips outward.
source: In the transition between the non-conductive and conductive state of KCNQ1, the proline pulls away from its position close to W304 and W305 and flips outward (Video 2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Video 2.

claim: Hydrogen bonds between W304-D317 and W305-Y315 and the proline interactions are likely absent in the non-conductive conformation of KCNQ1.
source: We hypothesize that those hydrogen bonds between W304-D317 and W305-Y315 and the proline interactions are likely absent in the non-conductive conformation of KCNQ1, thereby generating the high number of empty sweeps in control conditions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and single-channel data.

claim: The binding of Lin-Glycine to K326 and D301 at Site II biases the transition toward the conductive conformation, thereby increasing the number of non-empty sweeps and increasing Gmax.
source: We hypothesize that the binding of Lin-Glycine to K326 and D301 at Site II biases the transition toward the conductive conformation, thereby increasing the number of non-empty sweeps and increasing Gmax.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on all the data presented in the study.

claim: Mutations of residues involved in hydrogen bonds in the selectivity filter greatly reduce or abolish the Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine.
source: We here show that mutations of residues involved in these hydrogen bonds in the selectivity filter greatly reduce or abolish the Gmax effect of Lin-Glycine, as if Lin-Glycine increases the Gmax by stabilizing a conductive state of the selectivity filter through these hydrogen bonds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: In Shaker, the proline residue sits in between the two tryptophan residues and stabilizes the aromatic ring cuff.
source: For instance, in Shaker, the proline residue sits in between the two tryptophan residues and stabilizes the aromatic ring cuff (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In KCNQ1 the proline is positioned a little further outward and away from the two tryptophan residues, thus generating a looser arrangement of the aromatic ring cuff.
source: In contrast, in KCNQ1 the proline is positioned a little further outward and away from the two tryptophan residues, thus generating a looser arrangement of the aromatic ring cuff (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The difference in the stability of the aromatic cuff between Shaker and KCNQ1 might explain why the effect of PUFA on Gmax is large for KCNQ1 but not seen in Shaker.
source: This difference in the stability of the aromatic cuff between Shaker and KCNQ1 might explain why the effect of PUFA on Gmax is large for KCNQ1 but not seen in Shaker (Börjesson et al., 2008; Börjesson and Elinder, 2011) even if the residues involved in the Gmax effect are conserved between these two channels.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural differences and cited observations, supported by citations to Börjesson et al., 2008; Börjesson and Elinder, 2011.

claim: The KCNQ1/KCNE1 switches slowly (>10 s) between conductive and non-conductive states.
source: Our single-channel data show that the KCNQ1/KCNE1 switches slowly (>10 s) between conductive and non-conductive states, giving rise to many empty sweeps and few active sweeps.
evidence: This is based on single-channel data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Once the channel becomes conductive during a depolarization, the channel stays conductive for the remainder of the sweep.
source: However, once the channel becomes conductive during a depolarization, the channel stays conductive for the remainder of the sweep (see, e.g., Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for 20 s sweeps), as if VSD activation stabilizes the conductive state.
evidence: This is based on single-channel data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The selectivity filter is stabilized more in the non-conductive state when VSD is resting but stabilized more in the conductive state when VSD is activated.
source: Therefore, we propose a model in which the selectivity filter is stabilized more in the non-conductive state when VSD is resting but stabilized more in the conductive state when VSD is activated.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on single-channel data and structural analysis.

claim: The KCNQ1 structure with VSD resting was obtained in a low K+ solution.
source: The KCNQ1 structure with VSD resting was obtained in a low K+ solution, which in other Kv channels would promote C-type inactivation of the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is based on the methods described in Mandala and MacKinnon, 2023.

claim: It is the resting state of the VSD, and not the low K+, that caused the non-conductive selectivity filter in the KCNQ1 structure.
source: However, we think it is the resting state of the VSD, and not the low K+, that caused the non-conductive selectivity filter in the KCNQ1 structure because a KCNQ1 structure with VSD activated in the low K+ solution had a selectivity filter that was nearly identical to the KCNQ1 structure in high K+ with VSD activated (except for fewer K+ ions in the filter in low K+ solutions) (see Suppl. Figs. S5C and S5D in Mandala and MacKinnon, 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of structures from Mandala and MacKinnon, 2023.

claim: Currents from KCNQ1/KCNE1 channels display little external K+ dependence.
source: Note also the currents from KCNQ1/KCNE1 channels display little external K+ dependence (a small inhibition in addition to what is expected from changes in driving force) and that KCNQ1 channels are more strongly inhibited by high extracellular K+ concentrations (Abrahamyan et al., 2023; Larsen et al., 2011) in contrast to other Kv channels, such as Shaker K+ channels, which are inactivated more in low K+ (Larsson and Elinder, 2000; Kurata and Fedida, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abrahamyan et al., 2023; Larsen et al., 2011; Larsson and Elinder, 2000; Kurata and Fedida, 2006.

claim: The mechanism of PUFAs to increase KCNQ1/KCNE1 maximum conductance relies on the ability of PUFAs to favor the conductive conformation of the selectivity filter.
source: Our studies suggest that the mechanism of PUFAs to increase KCNQ1/KCNE1 maximum conductance relies on the ability of PUFAs to favor the conductive conformation of the selectivity filter: PUFAs promote interactions between residues in the selectivity filter that stabilize the channel pore.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the data presented.

claim: A crevice between K326 and D301 is present in structures of KCNQ1 with activated VSD but not in structures where the VSD is in the resting state.
source: Furthermore, we identify a crevice between K326 and D301 that is present in structures of KCNQ1 with activated VSD but not in structures where the VSD is in the resting state.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: PUFA binding in the crevice between K326 and D301 stabilizes the network of interactions that form the conductive form of the selectivity filter.
source: We propose that PUFA binding in this crevice stabilizes the network of interactions that form the conductive form of the selectivity filter.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the data and structural analysis.
